title: A Match Made in Vietnam
bodyHtml:
Below on the left are 23 words and phrases in Vietnamese, with their English translations on the right. The translations are in a different order than the original Vietnamese entries.

Vietnamese
1.băng
2.bó
3.bó hoa
4.cánh hoa
5.đá
6.đá lửa
7.đá phấn
8.đường
9.đường vòng
10.hoa
11.lửa
12.mở
13.mở đường
14.mở mắt
15.núi
16.núi băng
17.núi lửa
18.nước đá
19.nước mắt
20.phấn
21.phấn hoa
22.vòng
23.vòng hoa
English
A.bouquet (a bunch of flowers)
B.chalk
C.circle
D.cluster
E.detour
F.fire
G.flint (a stone used to make sparks)
H.flower
I.ice
J.iceberg
K.mountain
L.petal
M.pollen
N.powder
O.road
P.rock
Q.tear (as in teardrop)
R.to make aware
S.to open
T.to pave the way
U.volcano
V.wreath

Answer the following questions in the Answer Sheets:

F1. Match the Vietnamese entries to their English translations.

Note: One of the English translations will be used twice.

Hint: The Vietnamese word for “wing” is “cánh.” The Vietnamese word for “water” is “nước.”

F2. What is the English translation of “mắt”?

questions.partPrompt: Match the Vietnamese entries to their English translations. Give the letter (A-V) of the English translation. One of the English translations will be used twice. Hint: the Vietnamese word for "wing" is "cánh"; the Vietnamese word for "water" is "nước".
What is the English translation of "mắt"?

hints.text: Sort the Vietnamese list into one-word entries and two-word entries. Every two-word entry is built out of words that also appear on their own somewhere in the list (or that the problem's hint tells you about). Match the short ones first, since their English translations are the plainest words in the right-hand column.

Each two-word entry is a compound: one word names the general thing you are talking about, the other narrows it down. Work out which position carries the general meaning by testing a compound whose English translation you can guess, then apply the same order everywhere. The English translations of compounds are often single everyday words rather than literal two-word phrases, so translate the compound literally first and then ask which English word means that.

Here is the same reasoning on data outside this list. English builds compounds the other way round from Vietnamese: in "houseboat" the last part, "boat", tells you what kind of object it is, and "house" only describes it. In Vietnamese the describing word comes second instead. So if you know a language has a word for "water" and a word for "eye" but never combines them in English order, the combination beginning with the general word will literally read "water of the eye" - and then you look in the English column for the ordinary one-word name of that substance. Notice also that 23 Vietnamese entries share only 22 English translations, so exactly two entries mean the same thing.

explanationHtml:
What kind of puzzle is this?

Twenty-three Vietnamese items, twenty-two English translations, and no glossary. The way in is that most of the Vietnamese items are compounds: two words stuck together to name something new. Almost every word used inside a compound also appears by itself somewhere in the list, so you can solve the list from the inside out.

Step 1: split the list

Single words: băng, bó, đá, đường, hoa, lửa, mở, núi, phấn, vòng. Everything else is two words. The problem also hands you two words that never appear alone: cánh = wing and nước = water.

Step 2: find the order inside a compound

Look at hoa, which turns up in four compounds, always as the second word: bó hoa, cánh hoa, phấn hoa, vòng hoa. The English column has a set of flower-related words: bouquet, petal, pollen, wreath - and none of these is a flower. A bouquet is a bunch, a petal is a part shaped like a wing, pollen is a powder, a wreath is a ring. So in Vietnamese the first word names the thing and the second word tells you what it belongs to: hoa is the modifier, "of flowers". That is the opposite of English, where in "houseboat" the last part tells you it is a boat.

Now the flower group falls out. bó on its own must be "cluster", so bó hoa is literally "flower cluster" - a bouquet. vòng is "circle", so vòng hoa is a "flower circle" - a wreath. phấn is "powder", so phấn hoa is "flower powder" - pollen. And with the hint that cánh is "wing", cánh hoa is a "flower wing" - a petal.

Step 3: the same trick with rock, fire, ice and mountain

The single words đá, lửa, băng, núi match the plain English words rock, fire, ice, mountain - the question is which is which. Test the compounds:

  • núi lửa = "fire mountain" and núi băng = "ice mountain". English has exactly two words for those: volcano and iceberg. That fixes núi = mountain, lửa = fire, băng = ice.
  • So đá = rock, and đá lửa is a "fire rock" - flint, the stone you strike for sparks.
  • đá phấn is a "powder rock" - chalk.
  • nước đá is "rock water", i.e. water in a solid lump. English calls that ice - which is why one translation is used twice: it matches both băng and nước đá.

Step 4: roads, opening, and the leftover word

đường = road, so đường vòng is a "circle road" - a detour. mở = "to open", so mở đường is "to open a road" - to pave the way (an idiom: to make something possible for others).

That leaves mắt, which appears only inside compounds: mở mắt and nước mắt. Two English translations are still unused: "to make aware" and "tear (as in teardrop)". Since nước is water, nước mắt is "mắt-water" - and a teardrop is water from the eye. And mở mắt literally "to open mắt" matches "to make aware", exactly the English idiom "to open someone's eyes". So mắt means eye(s), which answers F2.

The big idea

Languages coin new words by combining old ones, and the two languages here put the pieces in opposite orders: Vietnamese is head-first (the general word comes first, its modifier second), English is head-last. Once you spot that, a two-word Vietnamese phrase can be translated literally and then matched to whatever single English word names the same thing.
_reviewNotes: Answer keys taken from the official solution page (F1 letters, F2 eye(s)). Booklet's English column prints longer glosses than the solution table (e.g. 'bouquet (a bunch of flowers)', 'flint (a stone used to make sparks)', 'tear (as in teardrop)'); keys are the letters, with the short word accepted as a variant. Points split 0.6 per F1 item (13.8) plus 1.2 for F2 to total 15 - adjust if a different official breakdown is preferred. Vietnamese diacritics should be checked character by character (băng, bó, cánh, đá, lửa, đường, mở, mắt, núi, nước, phấn, vòng).
